teaser.en: Its name comes from upesi, 'quickly', because few trees fill a forest gap faster.

summary.en: *Mpesi*, the pigeonwood or charcoal tree, is a fast-growing pioneer of forest gaps, clearings and fallow land. It supplies poles, firewood and charcoal, and its bark and leaves are used for deworming and cough.

about.en: *Mpesi* is a shrub or tree up to 12 metres tall with drooping branchlets. The leaves are rough, with toothed edges, and their bases are lopsided. The fruits are tiny and black, and birds spread them widely, which helps the tree reach new clearings.

where.en: It is a pioneer: one of the first trees to grow in forest gaps, clearings and fallow fields. Anywhere land has been cleared and left, look for its quick young stands.

uses.en:
The wood is used for poles, firewood and charcoal, which is where the English name 'charcoal tree' comes from. The tree also gives shade.

The bark and leaves are used in traditional medicine for deworming and for cough.

culture.en: Pakia explains the name *mpesi* as coming from *upesi*, 'quickly', because the tree grows so fast.

names.en: Pakia records two Digo names, *mpesi* and *mbonobono*; the ICRAF handbook also gives *mbonobono*, a name it uses as well for the orange-milk tree, *mkonotsaka*. In Swahili it is *mpesi*, and in Giriama *mzunguzungu*. In English it is pigeonwood or the charcoal tree.

reason.en: Also used for firewood and charcoal

sources: Pakia, M. (2005) African Traditional Plant Knowledge Today: an ethnobotanical study of the Digo at the Kenya Coast. PhD thesis, Univ. Bayreuth, Appendix III (Digo–botanical name list) & Appendix VI (name semantics). https://epub.uni-bayreuth.de/881/1/Pakia.pdf
